knowledge_statements.title: Factorable Algebraic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive algebraic representation used by deterministic continuous global solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is factorable over \(D\) if it admits a finite directed acyclic expression graph whose leaves are variables or constants and whose internal nodes apply arithmetic operations or specified univariate elementary functions. Every intermediate operation must be defined at each point of \(D\). A factorable optimization model represents its objective and constraint functions by such graphs, thereby exposing intermediate variables on which valid relaxations or range bounds can be constructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorable model gives every objective and constraint as a finite expression graph of arithmetic and elementary univariate operations, with all intermediate expressions defined on the search domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
The permitted elementary-function library is fixed.
Every intermediate expression is defined throughout \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has a finite factorable expression graph over \(D\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Derivative Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic derivative-access regime on an open neighborhood of the search domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(U\supseteq D\) be open. A first-order smooth derivative model for \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) consists of exact evaluation access to \(f(x)\) and \(\nabla f(x)\) for every \(x\in U\), with \(f\in C^1(U)\). A second-order model additionally returns \(\nabla^2 f(x)\) and requires \(f\in C^2(U)\). The declared order determines which derivative information a solver may use for local search, bounding, or stationarity tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth derivative model supplies exact values and derivatives of a continuously differentiable function; a second-order model also supplies the Hessian.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(U\) open.
Function and derivative evaluations are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(x\mapsto(f(x),
abla f(x))\), or \(x\mapsto(f(x),
abla f(x),
abla^2f(x))\), is available on \(U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-oracle regime with a supplied global Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a declared norm. A Lipschitz oracle model for \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) provides exact values \(f(x)\) at queried points and a valid constant \(L\geq0\) satisfying \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in D.\] Consequently, after observing \(f(x)\), the function \(y\mapsto f(x)-L\|y-x\|\) is a valid global lower support function on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns exact function values and a valid Lipschitz constant, yielding a cone-shaped global lower bound from every sampled point.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
The norm and valid constant \(L\) are supplied.
Oracle values are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)\geq f(x)-L\|y-x\|\) for all \(x,y\in D\).

notation.meaning: declared norm on the ambient space

knowledge_statements.title: Interval-Extension Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion-isotonic interval access for rigorous range enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(\mathcal{B}(D)\) denote the axis-aligned boxes contained in \(D\). An interval extension of \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is a map \(F:\mathcal{B}(D)\to\mathcal{I}(\mathbb{R})\) satisfying \[\{f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq F(X)\] for every \(X\in\mathcal{B}(D)\). It is inclusion isotonic if \(X\subseteq Y\) implies \(F(X)\subseteq F(Y)\), and point-consistent if \(F([x,x])=[f(x),f(x)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval extension maps every box to an interval containing the function’s entire range there; isotonicity preserves box inclusion and point consistency recovers exact values.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
\(F(X)\) is a real interval for each admissible box \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\) for every \(X\in\mathcal{B}(D)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budgeted black-box regime in which oracle calls dominate computational cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a search domain and let an oracle return information \(O(x)\) at query \(x\in D\) with declared cost \(c(x)>0\). Under total evaluation budget \(B>0\), a query sequence \((x_k)_{k=1}^N\) is feasible only if \[\sum_{k=1}^{N}c(x_k)\leq B.\] The access regime is called expensive when workflow complexity is accounted for primarily by this accumulated oracle cost, rather than by arithmetic performed between queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expensive access assigns a positive cost to each oracle call and restricts the query sequence by a total evaluation budget.
assumptions_latex: \(c(x)>0\) for every admissible query \(x\).
A finite total budget \(B>0\) is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k=1}^{N}c(x_k)\leq B\) is the admissibility condition for oracle queries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a finite point set relative to a polynomial space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set $\{\mathbf{x}^1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}^k\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is $\mathbb{R}_m[\mathbf{x}]$-unisolvent if every $q\in\mathbb{R}_m[\mathbf{x}]$ satisfying $q(\mathbf{x}^j)=0$ for all $j=1,\ldots,k$ is the null polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite point set is unisolvent for the polynomial space when the zero polynomial is the only polynomial in that space vanishing at every point.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf{x}^1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}^k\in\mathbb{R}^n
q\in\mathbb{R}_m[\mathbf{x}]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(q(\mathbf{x}^j)=0\ \forall j=1,\ldots,k\right)\Longrightarrow q\equiv0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential framework for optimization when objective evaluations are expensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose $k_0\ge 0$ and evaluate $f_k=f(\mathbf{x}_k)$ at selected $\mathbf{x}_k\in\mathbb{R}^n$ for $k=1,\ldots,k_0$, forming $S_{k_0}=\{(\mathbf{x}_i,f_i):1\le i\le k_0\}$, with $S_0=\varnothing$ if $k_0=0$. Starting with $k=k_0$, repeatedly construct a model $s(\cdot\mid S_k)$ of $f$, construct a merit function $\mathcal M(\cdot\mid S_k)$ depending on $s$, choose $\mathbf{x}_{k+1}\in\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal M(\mathbf{x}\mid S_k)$, evaluate $f_{k+1}=f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1})$, set $S_{k+1}=S_k\cup\{(\mathbf{x}_{k+1},f_{k+1})\}$, and increment $k$, until the stopping condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate an optional initial design, fit a surrogate to the observations, maximize a surrogate-dependent merit function to choose the next point, evaluate the true objective there, update the data set, and repeat until stopping.
assumptions_latex: k_0\ge 0
\mathbf{x}_k\in\mathbb{R}^n
S_0=\varnothing\text{ if }k_0=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf{x}_{k+1}\in\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal M(\mathbf{x}\mid S_k),\qquad S_{k+1}=S_k\cup\{(\mathbf{x}_{k+1},f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}))\}.

children.title: Noisy Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Workflow boundaries created by stochastic or contaminated evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic value-oracle regime with explicitly characterized observation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). A noisy value oracle queried at \(x\in D\) returns a random observation \(Y(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon(x)\), where the error law is part of the access specification. In the unbiased finite-variance regime, \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon(x)\mid x]=0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon(x)^2\mid x]\leq\sigma^2(x)<\infty\). The specification must also state whether errors from repeated or distinct queries are independent; without such a statement, independence is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noisy oracle returns a random perturbation of the true value, with bias, variance, and dependence assumptions explicitly declared.
assumptions_latex: \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is deterministic.
The conditional error distribution is defined for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon(x)\), with the error law and dependence structure specified.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stochastic observation model is precise and appropriately states that independence is not automatic, but it has no cited source supporting this exact access specification.

children.title: Cost–Noise Interaction
children.top_down_role: Regimes where limited evaluation budgets restrict noise management.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost–Noise Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replication tradeoff for independent unbiased observations of fixed per-call cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose repeated queries at \(x\) produce independent observations \(Y_i(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon_i(x)\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i(x)]=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i(x))=\sigma^2(x)\), and cost \(c(x)>0\) per query. For \(m\geq1\), the average \(\overline{Y}_m(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mY_i(x)\) has total cost \(mc(x)\), expectation \(f(x)\), and variance \(\sigma^2(x)/m\). Thus reducing standard deviation by a factor \(r>1\) through replication requires at least \(r^2\) times as many calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent replication reduces variance inversely with sample count while increasing cost linearly; dividing standard deviation by r requires r-squared times as many calls.
assumptions_latex: The repeated errors are independent and identically distributed.
\(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i(x)]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i(x))=\sigma^2(x)<\infty\).
Each query at \(x\) costs \(c(x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\overline{Y}_m(x)]=f(x)\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline{Y}_m(x))=\sigma^2(x)/m\), and \(\operatorname{cost}(\overline{Y}_m)=mc(x)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The replication cost and variance formulas are standard and the property content kind fits the interaction leaf, but no source is provided for the stated model and tradeoff.

children.title: Interval Domains

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional connected domains determined by two ordered endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For endpoints \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\) with \(a\leq b\), an interval domain is one of \([a,b]\), \((a,b)\), \([a,b)\), or \((a,b]\), according to the declared endpoint-inclusion convention. The closed interval is \([a,b]=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:a\leq x\leq b\}\). If \(a=b\), the closed interval is the singleton \(\{a\}\), whereas every convention excluding an endpoint yields the empty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval domain is the set between two ordered real endpoints, with each endpoint included or excluded according to a declared convention.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\)
\(a\leq b\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\in\{[a,b],(a,b),[a,b),(a,b]\}\) under the chosen boundary convention.

children.title: Axis-Aligned Box Domains
children.top_down_role: Cartesian box representations for multivariate subdivision.

knowledge_statements.title: Axis-Aligned Box Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian-product search domains aligned with the coordinate axes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(l_i\leq u_i\) for every \(i\). The closed axis-aligned box with lower corner \(l\) and upper corner \(u\) is \[ [l,u]=\prod_{i=1}^n[l_i,u_i]=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:l_i\leq x_i\leq u_i\text{ for all }i\}. \] It is full-dimensional exactly when \(l_i<u_i\) for all \(i\); otherwise it is a lower-dimensional, nonempty degenerate box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An axis-aligned box is a Cartesian product of coordinate intervals. It is full-dimensional exactly when every lower bound is strictly below its upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\)
\(l_i\leq u_i\) for all \(i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([l,u]=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:l\leq x\leq u\}\).

children.title: Box Boundary Conventions
children.top_down_role: Open, closed, bounded, or extended box conventions affecting solver interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Box Boundary Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint-inclusion and degeneracy conventions for Cartesian-product boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each coordinate \(i\), choose relations \(\triangleleft_i\in\{<,\leq\}\) and \(\triangleright_i\in\{<,\leq\}\). The corresponding box is \[B=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:l_i\mathbin{\triangleleft_i}x_i\mathbin{\triangleright_i}u_i\text{ for every }i\},\] where the left relation is read from \(l_i\) to \(x_i\). A workflow must declare these relations and its treatment of \(l_i=u_i\). Under the closed convention, equality produces a fixed coordinate; if either adjacent boundary is strict, that coordinate makes \(B\) empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box convention declares separately whether each lower and upper face is included and how equal coordinate bounds are treated.
assumptions_latex: \(l_i\leq u_i\) for every coordinate.
Each endpoint relation is explicitly chosen as strict or nonstrict.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is uniquely determined by \(l\), \(u\), and the declared endpoint relations.

notation.meaning: box under the declared boundary convention
lower and upper endpoint relations in coordinate i

knowledge_statements.title: Simplicial Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed simplices represented by affinely independent vertices or barycentric coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_0,\ldots,v_d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be affinely independent, so \(d\leq n\). The simplex generated by these vertices is \[S=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_d\}=\left\{\sum_{i=0}^d\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^d\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] It has affine dimension \(d\), and every \(x\in S\) has unique barycentric coordinates \((\lambda_0,
\ldots,\lambda_d)\). A simplicial search domain is such a simplex or a declared finite union of simplices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex is the convex hull of affinely independent vertices; its points have unique nonnegative barycentric coordinates summing to one.
assumptions_latex: \(v_0,\ldots,v_d\in\mathbb{R}^n\)
The vertices are affinely independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{\sum_{i=0}^d\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^d\lambda_i=1\}\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simplex and barycentric-coordinate claims are standard, but no source is cited. The plain statement also omits the LaTeX statement's extension from a single simplex to a declared finite union of simplices.

children.title: Bounded Polyhedral Domains
children.top_down_role: Polytope-based search regions used by global workflows.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Polyhedral Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty bounded intersections of finitely many closed affine halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bounded polyhedral domain is a nonempty set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) admitting a representation \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\] for some \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), such that \(P\) is bounded. Equivalently, its recession cone satisfies \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\leq0\}=\{0\}.\] Such a domain is a polytope and equals the convex hull of finitely many points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded polyhedral domain is a nonempty bounded intersection of finitely many closed halfspaces; equivalently, its recession cone contains only zero.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\)
\(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is bounded if and only if \(\{d:Ad\leq0\}=\{0\}\).

children.title: Unbounded Polyhedral Domains
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral regions requiring explicit recession handling.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Polyhedral Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedra represented by linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral domain is a nonempty set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Its recession cone is \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}\). The domain is unbounded exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\neq\{0\}\); equivalently, some \(x\in P\) and nonzero \(d\) satisfy \(x+td\in P\) for every \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty linear-inequality domain is unbounded exactly when it has a nonzero feasible recession direction along which an infinite ray remains feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(P\neq\varnothing\)
\(n,m<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is unbounded}\iff\operatorname{rec}(P)\neq\{0\}\).

children.title: Conical Domains
children.top_down_role: Cone-represented search regions encountered by relaxation workflows.

knowledge_statements.title: Conical Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex cones used as continuous search domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conical domain is a nonempty convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(\lambda x\in K\) for every \(x\in K\) and \(\lambda\ge0\). Equivalently, \(x,y\in K\) and \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\) imply \(\alpha x+\beta y\in K\). When topological closure is required by a solver, the domain is additionally assumed closed; pointedness and nonempty interior are separate properties, not consequences of conicality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conical domain is closed under nonnegative linear combinations. Closure, pointedness, and full dimensionality require separate assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x,y\in K,\ \alpha,\beta\ge0\Rightarrow\alpha x+\beta y\in K\).

children.title: Polyhedral–Conical Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Solver-facing transitions between inequality systems and cone representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral–Conical Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-cone decomposition of nonempty polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), its recession cone is the polyhedral cone \(C=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}\). There exist finite sets of points \(V\subseteq P\) and directions \(R\subseteq C\) such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R),\qquad C=\operatorname{cone}(R).\] Thus the bounded component is represented by convex combinations of \(V\), while every unbounded direction is represented through the conical component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty polyhedron decomposes into a polytope generated by finitely many points plus its finitely generated recession cone.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{rec}(P)\) for suitable finite \(V\), with \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\) finitely generated.

children.title: General Convex Domains
children.top_down_role: Convex search regions lacking a preferred box, simplex, or polyhedral representation.

knowledge_statements.title: General Convex Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex feasible regions without a prescribed representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A general convex domain is a nonempty set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) such that, for all \(x,y\in D\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y\in D\). The definition does not require \(D\) to be polyhedral, bounded, closed, or full-dimensional; any such property must be supplied separately in a solver specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain is convex when it contains the line segment joining every pair of its points; boundedness, closure, and representation are separate properties.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x,y\in D,\ \lambda\in[0,1]\Rightarrow(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y\in D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Star-Shaped Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Star-shaped domains and their kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is star-shaped if its kernel \[\ker(D)=\{c\in D:(1-t)c+tx\in D\text{ for every }x\in D\text{ and }t\in[0,1]\}\] is nonempty. Each \(c\in\ker(D)\) is a star center. Every convex domain is star-shaped and satisfies \(\ker(D)=D\), whereas a nonconvex star-shaped domain may have a proper, lower-dimensional kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain is star-shaped when some point sees every domain point along an entirely feasible line segment; all such centers form its kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\text{ is star-shaped}\iff\ker(D)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: set of star centers of D

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity-Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle representation of a closed convex search domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A strong separation oracle for \(D\) maps a query \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) either to the declaration \(x\in D\), or to \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}y\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}x\) for every \(y\in D\). Oracle access represents \(D\) operationally without requiring an explicit finite inequality description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle either confirms membership or returns a hyperplane strictly separating the query point from the closed convex domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin D\Rightarrow\exists(a,\beta):a^{\mathsf T}y\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}x\ \forall y\in D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-separation-oracle formulation is standard and internally precise, but no inspectable citation is supplied to support the selected oracle model and its assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel-Dependent Search Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial feasibility geometry induced by a chosen star center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be star-shaped and choose \(c\in\ker(D)\). For every direction \(u\) with \(\lVert u\rVert_2=1\), define \(\rho_c(u)=\sup\{r\ge0:c+su\in D\text{ for all }s\in[0,r]\}\). Then every radial segment \(\{c+su:0\le s<\rho_c(u)\}\) lies in \(D\). Both \(\rho_c\) and any radial partition based on it may change when a different kernel point is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing a star center induces feasible radial intervals in every direction; their lengths and resulting search partitions generally depend on that center.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is star-shaped
\(c\in\ker(D)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le s<\rho_c(u)\Rightarrow c+su\in D\).

notation.meaning: maximal guaranteed radial reach from c in direction u

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Value Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-error certification of a global optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v^*=\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\), a global-value certificate with tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\) consists of verified scalars \(L\) and \(U\) satisfying \(L\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in D\), \(U=f(\hat x)\) for some verified \(\hat x\in D\), and \(U-L\le\varepsilon\). It certifies \(v^*\in[L,U]\) and \(0\le U-v^*\le\varepsilon\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), it certifies the exact global value \(v^*=L=U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid global lower bound and a feasible objective value within epsilon certify an epsilon-wide enclosure of the global optimum value.
assumptions_latex: \(D\neq\varnothing\)
\(v^*=\inf_{x\in D}f(x)>-\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\le v^*\le U\ \text{ and }\ U-L\le\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound and feasible-upper-bound certificate is mathematically correct and matches the certification target, but the record supplies no source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Minimizer Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification of a feasible point as globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\neq\varnothing\) and \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). A global-minimizer certificate for \(\hat x\in D\) consists of verified feasibility of \(\hat x\) and a valid global lower bound \(L\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in D\). If \(f(\hat x)-L\le\varepsilon\), then \(f(\hat x)\le\inf_{x\in D}f(x)+\varepsilon\), so \(\hat x\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-global minimizer. With \(\varepsilon=0\), \(\hat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility plus a global lower bound matching the candidate value within epsilon certifies the point as epsilon-globally minimizing.
assumptions_latex: \(D\neq\varnothing\)
\(\hat x\in D\)
\(L\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in D\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\hat x)-L\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow f(\hat x)\le\inf_{x\in D}f(x)+\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate implication is standard, but no source is supplied. A sourced revision should also state explicitly that the optimality tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Infeasibility Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-cover exclusion certificate for continuous constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the feasible set \(F=\{x\in D:g_j(x)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), a global-infeasibility certificate consists of finitely many sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_N\) covering \(D\) and, for each \(B_i\), an index \(j(i)\) with a verified lower bound \(\ell_i>0\) such that \(g_{j(i)}(x)\ge\ell_i\) for every \(x\in B_i\cap D\). Every point of \(D\) then violates at least one constraint, and consequently \(F=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite cover certifies global infeasibility when every covered region has a rigorously positive lower bound for at least one violated constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N B_i\)
\(g_{j(i)}(x)\ge\ell_i>0\) for all \(x\in B_i\cap D\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: member of the finite domain cover

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-cover construction is a valid sufficient infeasibility certificate for inequality systems, but no inspectable source supports this particular certificate format.

knowledge_statements.title: All-Solution Enclosure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verified outer enclosure of every solution of a system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:D\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(Z=\{x\in D:F(x)=0\}\). An all-solution enclosure is a finite family of verified sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_N\subseteq D\) together with a verified exclusion of every point in \(D\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^N B_i\) from \(Z\). Consequently, \(Z\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N B_i\). If the sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_N\) are pairwise disjoint and each has a verified existence-and-uniqueness certificate for a zero of \(F\), then they isolate all solutions, exactly one in each enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Verified exclusion outside finitely many sets encloses every solution. If the enclosures are pairwise disjoint and each is certified to contain exactly one solution, they isolate all solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
\(F:D\to\mathbb{R}^m\)
\(F(x)\neq0\) for every \(x\in D\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^N B_i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N B_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Piyavskii–Shubert Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic univariate Lipschitz global minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an \(L\)-Lipschitz function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and initial samples \(x_1=a,x_2=b\), maintain \(q_k(x)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\{f(x_i)-L|x-x_i|\}\), \(L_k=\min_{x\in[a,b]}q_k(x)\), and \(U_k=\min_i f(x_i)\). If \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\), return a sampled minimizer attaining \(U_k\). Otherwise choose \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in[a,b]}q_k(x)\), evaluate \(f(x_{k+1})\), and repeat. The returned point is \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method repeatedly samples where the Lipschitz lower envelope is smallest and stops when its best value and the incumbent differ by at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|\) for all \(x,y\in[a,b]\)
\(\varepsilon>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\hat x)-\min_{x\in[a,b]}f(x)\le\varepsilon\) at termination.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz lower envelope after k samples

knowledge_statements.title: Kushner Partition Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic univariate Lipschitz branch-and-bound form of the Kushner partition family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Initialize a finite interval partition \(\mathcal P_0\) containing \([a,b]\), evaluate its endpoints, and assign every \(I=[u,v]\) a valid lower bound \(B(I)\le \min_{x\in I}f(x)\), computed from the sampled values and \(L\). At iteration \(k\), select an interval minimizing \(B(I)\), evaluate \(f\) at an interior point, and replace that interval by the resulting subintervals. Maintain \(U_k\) as the smallest sampled value and stop when \(U_k-\min_{I\in\mathcal P_k}B(I)\le\varepsilon\); return the sample attaining \(U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly split the interval having the best Lipschitz lower bound, update the incumbent sample, and stop when the certified lower–upper gap is within tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with known \(L>0\).
Every selected interval is split at a strict interior point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_k-\min_{I\in\mathcal P_k}B(I)\le\varepsilon\) certifies that the returned value is at most \(\varepsilon\) above \(\min_{x\in[a,b]}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: valid lower bound on interval I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential univariate global search under a stochastic-process model, with a Wiener-process interval-priority specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Model \(f(x)=\varphi(x,\omega)\) for every \(x\in D\), for some fixed \(\omega\) in a probability space, and let \(S_k=\{(x_i,z_i):z_i=f(x_i),\ i=0,\ldots,k\}\). A one-step Bayes strategy selects \(x_{k+1}\in\arg\operatorname{opt}_{x\in D}\mathbb E[U(\varphi(x,\omega)\mid S_k)]\). One instance, for \(\varepsilon>0\), is \(x_{k+1}\in\arg\max_{x\in D}\mathbb P\{\varphi(x,\omega)<f_k^\star-\varepsilon\mid S_k\}\), where \(f_k^\star=\min_{1\le j\le k}z_j\). For ordered samples on \(D=[0,1]\), if the model is a Wiener process with increments of mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2|x_1-x_2|\), \(\sigma>0\), the corresponding interval partition operator is \(P_i=\exp\{-2(f_k^\star-\varepsilon-z_i)(f_k^\star-\varepsilon-z_{i-1})/[\sigma^2(x_i-x_{i-1})]\}\). This operator can be used to select intervals in a sequential partition algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treat the objective as one realization of a random function and update the conditional model using sampled points. A one-step Bayesian rule chooses the next evaluation by optimizing conditional expected utility; one stated criterion maximizes the probability of improving the current sample minimum by more than epsilon. Under a Wiener-process model on [0,1], the displayed exponential quantity is the associated interval-priority operator.
assumptions_latex: f(x)=\varphi(x,\omega)\quad\forall x\in D\text{ for some fixed }\omega\in\Omega
S_k=\{(x_i,z_i):z_i=f(x_i),\ i=0,\ldots,k\}
\varepsilon>0
D=[0,1]\text{ and the samples are ordered for the Wiener-process partition specialization}
\varphi(x_1,\omega)-\varphi(x_2,\omega)\sim N(0,\sigma^2|x_1-x_2|)
\sigma>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}\in\arg\max_{x\in D}\mathbb P\!\left\{\varphi(x,\omega)<f_k^\star-\varepsilon\mid S_k\right\},\qquad P_i=\exp\!\left(-\frac{2(f_k^\star-\varepsilon-z_i)(f_k^\star-\varepsilon-z_{i-1})}{\sigma^2(x_i-x_{i-1})}\right)

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Interval-Partition Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic certified adaptive partition scheme for univariate global minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\), an interval lower-bounding rule \(B\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), initialize \(\mathcal P_0=\{[a,b]\}\) and evaluate the samples required by \(B\). At iteration \(k\), let \(U_k\) be the best sampled value, choose any active \(I_k\in\mathcal P_k\) with smallest lower bound, and subdivide \(I_k\) whenever \(B(I_k)<U_k-\varepsilon\). Discard every interval satisfying \(B(I)\ge U_k-\varepsilon\). Stop when no active interval remains; output a sampled point attaining \(U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptively refine only intervals whose lower bounds can still improve the incumbent by more than the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(B(I)\le\inf_{x\in I}f(x)\) for every generated interval \(I\).
The generated active intervals cover every point not discarded by the bound test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, the returned point \(\hat x\) satisfies \(f(\hat x)-\min_{x\in[a,b]}f(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: certified lower bound for interval I

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Partition Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axis-aligned rectangular branch-and-bound for a compact box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]\), and suppose a bound \(B(R)\le\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\) is available for every generated axis-aligned rectangle \(R\subseteq D\). Initialize \(\mathcal P_0=\{D\}\). At iteration \(k\), maintain the incumbent sampled value \(U_k\), select an active rectangle having minimum \(B(R)\), and split it by coordinate hyperplanes into finitely many rectangles with union \(R\) and pairwise disjoint interiors. Prune each rectangle satisfying \(B(R)\ge U_k-\varepsilon\). When no active rectangle remains, return a sampled point attaining \(U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition a box into axis-aligned rectangles, refine the rectangle with the smallest certified lower bound, and prune cells that cannot improve the incumbent by more than the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty compact box, \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
Every generated bound \(B(R)\) is valid, every split covers its parent, and \(U_k\) is the value of a sampled feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(U_k-\min_{x\in D}f(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: valid lower bound on cell R

knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Partition Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangular partition using diagonal endpoint information for selection and subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a compact box \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\), represent each active rectangle \(R=[u,v]\) by opposite vertices \(u,v\), its diagonal length \(d_R=\lVert v-u\rVert_2\), and a valid lower bound \(B_R\) derived from available diagonal samples. Initialize with \(D\). Repeatedly select a rectangle minimizing \(B_R\), evaluate any new diagonal subdivision points, and partition the selected rectangle into finitely many axis-aligned children whose union is \(R\) and whose interiors are pairwise disjoint. Prune a rectangle when \(B_R\ge U-\varepsilon\), and return the incumbent when every rectangle has been pruned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent boxes by opposite vertices, use diagonal sample information to rank them, and subdivide promising boxes while maintaining certified lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty compact box, \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
Each \(B_R\) is a valid lower bound on \(R\), and \(U\) is the value of a sampled feasible point.
Along every infinite selected descendant chain, the diagonal lengths tend to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the algorithm terminates, its incumbent satisfies \(U-\min_{x\in D}f(x)\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characteristic-driven diagonal partition scheme for global optimization over a hyperinterval; the extract supplies no convergence or global-optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the search hyperinterval \(D=[a,b]\), evaluate \(x^1=a\) and \(x^2=b\), set \(z^j=f(x^j)\), \(p(1)=2\), \(\{D^1\}=\{D\}\), \(M(1)=1\), and \(k=1\). If \(\|a_t-b_t\|\le\varepsilon\|a-b\|\), stop and return \(z_k^*=\min_{1\le j\le p(k)}z^j\) together with a sampled point \(x_k^*\in\arg\min_{1\le j\le p(k)}f(x^j)\). Otherwise, use the partition strategy \(P\) to replace \(D_t\) by \(\Delta M(k)>1\) hyperintervals, perform \(\Delta p(k)\) new trials at vertices associated with their main diagonals, set \(p(k+1)=p(k)+\Delta p(k)\) and \(M(k+1)=M(k)+\Delta M(k)-1\), increment \(k\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the endpoints of the initial box's main diagonal. At every iteration, compute a parameterized characteristic for each current box and select a box with maximum characteristic. If its diagonal is at most epsilon times the initial diagonal, return the best sampled point and value. Otherwise, replace the selected box with more than one new box, evaluate the prescribed vertices of their main diagonals, update the trial and box counts, and repeat.

P\text{ replaces the selected hyperinterval by }\Delta M(k)>1\text{ new hyperintervals.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The scheme repeatedly partitions a maximum-characteristic hyperinterval until the selected diagonal satisfies }\|a_t-b_t\|\le\varepsilon\|a-b\|,\text{ then returns the best sampled incumbent.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdivision and partition-update rule for a selected hyperinterval in a diagonal global-optimization partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R^N\) be an \(N\)-dimensional hypercube, and let \(D_t=[a_t,b_t]\) be selected from the partition at iteration \(k\ge 1\). Choose \(i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{1\le j\le N}|b_t(j)-a_t(j)|\). Define \(u\) by replacing \(a_t(i)\) with \(a_t(i)+\tfrac23(b_t(i)-a_t(i))\), and define \(v\) by replacing \(b_t(i)\) with \(b_t(i)+\tfrac23(a_t(i)-b_t(i))\). Obtain \(f(u)\) and \(f(v)\), either by evaluation or lookup, and cut \(D_t\) with the two coordinate hyperplanes through these points perpendicular to coordinate \(i\). Replace \(D_t\) by three equal hyperintervals whose main-diagonal endpoint pairs are \((u,v)\), \((a_t,v)\), and \((u,b_t)\), leaving all other hyperintervals unchanged. If exactly one hyperinterval is subdivided, then \(M(k+1)=M(k)+2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a hyperinterval and one of its longest coordinate edges. Form trial points at the two trisection locations, obtain their objective values, and cut perpendicular to that edge through the points. Replace the selected hyperinterval by three equal hyperintervals with diagonal endpoint pairs (u,v), (a_t,v), and (u,b_t). All other hyperintervals remain unchanged, and the partition size increases by two.
assumptions_latex: D=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R^N\text{ is an }N\text{-dimensional hypercube}
k\ge 1
D_t=[a_t,b_t]\text{ is selected from the current partition}
i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{1\le j\le N}|b_t(j)-a_t(j)|
\text{exactly one hyperinterval is subdivided at iteration }k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_t\text{ is replaced by three equal hyperintervals and }M(k+1)=M(k)+2.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplicial Partition Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-and-bound over a conforming simplicial partition of a compact polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a compact polytope \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) have an initial finite triangulation \(\mathcal T_0\). For each generated simplex \(S\), compute a valid lower bound \(B(S)\). At iteration \(k\), select an active simplex of minimum bound, subdivide it by a conforming rule such as longest-edge bisection, evaluate the required new sample points, and update the incumbent \(U_k\). Remove every simplex satisfying \(B(S)\ge U_k-\varepsilon\). Stop when no active simplex remains, and return a sampled point attaining \(U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Triangulate the domain, refine a simplex with minimum certified lower bound, and prune simplices that cannot improve the incumbent beyond the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a compact polytope admitting a finite triangulation, \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
Each \(B(S)\) is a valid lower bound on \(S\), and \(U_k\) is the value of a sampled feasible point.
Repeated refinement drives the diameters to zero along every infinite selected descendant chain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(U_k-\min_{x\in D}f(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: active simplicial partition at iteration k
valid lower bound on simplex S

knowledge_statements.title: Conical Partition Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition of a star-shaped domain by finitely many directional cones sharing an apex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact and star-shaped with respect to \(v\in D\). A conical partition of \(D\) is a finite family \(\{D_j\}_{j=1}^m\) for which \(D_j=D\cap(v+C_j)\), where every \(C_j\) is a closed convex cone with apex at the origin, \(\bigcup_{j=1}^m C_j\) contains every direction \(x-v\) with \(x\in D\), and distinct cells have disjoint relative interiors. Thus \(D=\bigcup_{j=1}^mD_j\); cellwise lower bounds may consequently be combined as \(B(D)=\min_j B(D_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A star-shaped domain is covered by directionally separated cone cells sharing a common apex, permitting independent cell bounds and refinement.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is compact and star-shaped with respect to \(v\).
Each \(B(D_j)\le\inf_{x\in D_j}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D=\bigcup_{j=1}^mD_j\) and \(\min_jB(D_j)\le\min_{x\in D}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained stochastic search combining equality-constraint preprocessing with adaptive Gaussian trial generation; no global-convergence guarantee is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: ICRS first reorders the equality constraints using an occurrence matrix so that as many unknowns as possible are computed sequentially, solving remaining coupled subsets simultaneously. Starting from a user-specified or automatically generated feasible point, it samples trial points from a Gaussian distribution with componentwise standard deviations determined by the current decision vector, variable bounds, and \(k_1\) (default \(k_1=1/3\)). Each trial is tested by solving the equalities—using modified Newton--Raphson for coupled subsets—and checking the inequalities. After \(\eta_e n\) unsuccessful trials, the standard-deviation vector is multiplied by \(k_2\) (defaults \(k_2=1/2\), \(\eta_e=25\)); an improving feasible trial starts a new iteration and updates the standard deviations. Termination uses prescribed objective and decision-variable tolerances. The equality-solving stage may be unreliable near singular points, in strongly nonlinear regions, or when the decision vector produces a nearly singular Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: ICRS first orders and reduces the equality equations so that variables are computed sequentially where possible and coupled equation subsets are solved together when necessary. It then performs constrained random search from a supplied or automatically generated feasible point, drawing bound-aware Gaussian trials. Equalities are solved and inequalities checked for every trial. After 25n unsuccessful trials by default, the sampling standard deviations are halved; an improving feasible trial starts the next iteration. The method stops using objective and variable tolerances. Equality solution can be problematic near singularities, highly nonlinear regions, or nearly singular Jacobians.
assumptions_latex: n\text{ is the number of decision variables}
\ell\le \mathbf X\le u\text{ supplies lower and upper variable bounds}
k_1=\tfrac13,\quad k_2=\tfrac12,\quad \eta_e=25\text{ by default}
\text{Feasibility is tested by solving }\mathbf H(\mathbf X)=0\text{ and checking }\mathbf G(\mathbf X)\le0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{After }\eta_e n\text{ unsuccessful trials, }\boldsymbol\sigma\leftarrow k_2\boldsymbol\sigma;\text{ an improving feasible trial initiates the next iteration.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic specification only; it gives no convergence or global-optimality guarantee and explicitly limits attainable precision through a finite grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^d$, assign each dyadic coordinate $x_i=\pm\sum_{j=1}^{\ell_i}a_j2^{-j}$, with $a_j\in\{0,1\}$ and $a_{\ell_i}=1$ when $x_i\ne0$, the level $\ell_i$ (and assign $0$ level $0$), and set $\operatorname{level}(x)=\sum_i\ell_i$. Initialize $X=\{0\}$. For each sampled $x\in X$, let $\operatorname{degree}(x)$ be one plus its previous selection count and let $\operatorname{rank}(x)=\#\{y\in\{f(z):z\in X\}:y\le f(x)\}$. Given $\alpha\in[0,1]$, select an eligible $\widetilde x\in X$ minimizing $g(x)=(\operatorname{level}(x)+\operatorname{degree}(x))^\alpha\operatorname{rank}(x)^{1-\alpha}$; if its current degree is $m$, sample every in-domain neighbor differing in one coordinate by $\pm2^{-\operatorname{level}(\widetilde x_i)-m}$. Then increment $\operatorname{degree}(\widetilde x)$ and recompute ranks. Restrict coordinate levels to $k_0$, yielding at most $N=(2^{k_0}+1)^d$ grid points. If a sampled point is smaller than all nearest grid neighbors at distance $2^{-k_0}$, exclude a centered box of side length $\varepsilon$, $0\le\varepsilon<1$, from future selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transform a hyperrectangle affinely to the centered unit box, initialize at the origin, and iteratively refine dyadic hyperbolic-cross points. At each iteration select the sampled eligible point minimizing a score that balances its total dyadic level plus prior selection count against its objective-value rank, then evaluate all in-domain neighbors at the point's current refinement degree. Update its degree and all ranks afterward. Cap coordinate levels by the fineness parameter k0, and after detecting a grid-local minimum exclude a centered box of side length epsilon from future selections. Alpha equal to 1 gives nonadaptive level-driven behavior, whereas alpha equal to 0 strongly favors low-ranked objective values. The finite grid generally does not provide a high-precision global optimum.
assumptions_latex: f:[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^d\to\mathbb R\text{ is evaluable at the sampled grid points}
\alpha\in[0,1],\quad k_0\in\mathbb N_0,\quad 0\le\varepsilon<1
x_i=\pm\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j2^{-j},\quad a_j\in\{0,1\},\quad k\le k_0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure generates an adaptive sequence of at most }(2^{k_0}+1)^d\text{ dyadic-grid samples and returns the sampled point with minimum observed }f\text{-value, without asserting exact global optimality.}

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Grid Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz error guarantee and sample count for a Cartesian grid on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm, and let \(G\subset D\) be a finite Cartesian grid with fill distance \(\rho=\sup_{x\in D}\min_{g\in G}\lVert x-g\rVert_2\). If \(\hat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in G}f(g)\), then \(0\le f(\hat x)-\min_{x\in D}f(x)\le L\rho\). For \(L>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), set \(N_j=\left\lceil L\sqrt n\,(b_j-a_j)/(2\varepsilon)\right\rceil\) and use \(N_j+1\) equally spaced points, including both endpoints, in coordinate \(j\). This grid has \(\rho\le\varepsilon/L\) and uses \(\prod_{j=1}^n(N_j+1)\) evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Cartesian grid gives objective error at most the Lipschitz constant times its fill distance. Choosing the displayed number of equal coordinate subdivisions guarantees error at most epsilon, with exponentially dimension-dependent sampling cost.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty compact box and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm.
\(L>0\), \(\varepsilon>0\), function evaluations are exact, and both coordinate endpoints are included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed grid satisfies \(f(\hat x)-\min_{x\in D}f(x)\le\varepsilon\) and has \(\prod_{j=1}^n\left(\left\lceil L\sqrt n\,(b_j-a_j)/(2\varepsilon)\right\rceil+1\right)\) points.

notation.meaning: Euclidean fill distance of G in D
number of equal subdivisions in coordinate j

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Covering Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Lipschitz bounds obtained from a finite metric-ball cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((D,d)\) be a compact metric space, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz, and suppose \(D\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^m\{x\in D:d(x,c_i)\le r_i\}\), where \(c_i\in D\) and \(r_i\ge0\). Define \(U=\min_{1\le i\le m}f(c_i)\) and \(B=\min_{1\le i\le m}\{f(c_i)-Lr_i\}\). For every \(x\in D\), membership in a covering ball implies \(f(x)\ge B\). Hence \(B\le f^*\le U\), where \(f^*=\min_{x\in D}f(x)\), and the cover data and sampled values form a directly checkable certificate of the gap \(U-B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite metric-ball cover and a Lipschitz constant convert center evaluations into checkable global lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: \((D,d)\) is a compact metric space, and the displayed closed balls cover \(D\).
\(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\le\min_{x\in D}f(x)\le U\); if \(U-B\le\varepsilon\), then a center attaining \(U\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.

notation.meaning: center and radius of covering ball i

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Cover Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-directed refinement of a finite geometric cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be compact, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and start from a finite cover \(\mathcal C_0=\{C_i\}\) of \(D\), with a sampled feasible point and a valid lower bound \(B(C_i)\le\inf_{x\in C_i}f(x)\) for each cell. At iteration \(k\), set \(U_k\) to the best sampled value, discard cells satisfying \(B(C_i)\ge U_k-\varepsilon\), and select a remaining cell of minimum bound. Replace the selected cell by finitely many smaller cells whose union covers it, and compute the required samples and bounds for the children. Stop when no cell remains eligible for refinement, and return a sampled point attaining \(U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refine only cover cells with competitive certified lower bounds, preserve coverage under replacement, and stop when every remaining region is excluded to the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is compact, \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
Every replacement covers its parent, every cell bound is valid, and \(U_k\) is the value of a sampled feasible point.
Along every infinite refined descendant chain, the cell diameters tend to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At finite termination, \(U_k-\min_{x\in D}f(x)\le\varepsilon\).

valid lower bound for cover cell i

knowledge_statements.title: Cover Overlap Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe pruning and ownership rules for overlapping cover cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\) be a finite, possibly overlapping cover, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and suppose \(B_i\le\inf_{x\in C_i}f(x)\). A deterministic ownership rule may assign each currently unresolved point to one active cell containing it, allowing samples at shared points to be evaluated only once. A cell whose owned unresolved region is empty may be deleted only if the ownership assignments still cover every unresolved point. A cell satisfying \(B_i\ge U-\varepsilon\) may instead be marked certified and removed from the active set without reassignment. Thus every point remains either represented by an active containing cell or excluded by a valid tolerance certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For overlapping cells, ownership-based deletion must preserve coverage of unresolved points, while a cell whose lower bound is already within tolerance may be removed as certified. Shared samples can be deduplicated.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\), \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and each \(B_i\) is a valid lower bound on \(C_i\).
\(U\) is the value of a sampled feasible point, and ownership is assigned only to active cells containing the relevant point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point is either covered by an active cell or belongs to a cell certified by \(B_i\ge U-\varepsilon\); consequently, if no active cell remains, then \(U-\min_{x\in D}f(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: valid lower bound for cell i

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposable Partition Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive finite partition operator with exact coverage and shrinking descendants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((D,d)\) be a metric space and let \(\mathcal K\) be a family of nonempty compact subsets of \(D\). A decomposable partition operator is a map \(P\) assigning each nonsingleton \(C\in\mathcal K\) a finite family \(P(C)=\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\subset\mathcal K\) such that \(C=\bigcup_{j=1}^m C_j\), distinct children have disjoint relative interiors, and every child is a proper subset of \(C\). The operator is exhaustive if every infinite descendant chain \(C_0\supset C_1\supset\cdots\), with \(C_{k+1}\in P(C_k)\), satisfies \(\operatorname{diam}(C_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposable operator replaces a nonsingleton cell by finitely many proper children that exactly partition it. It is exhaustive when every infinite descendant chain has vanishing diameter.
assumptions_latex: \((D,d)\) is a metric space, and every member of \(\mathcal K\) is a nonempty compact subset of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated application of an exhaustive \(P\) preserves the covered region and yields \(\operatorname{diam}(C_k)\to0\) along every infinite descendant chain.

notation.meaning: admissible family of nonempty compact cells
finite family of children of cell C

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Extension Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremal Lipschitz extensions and sample-based envelopes on a metric domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((D,d)\) be a metric space, let \(S=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subset D\), and let sampled values \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(|f_i-f_j|\le Ld(x_i,x_j)\) for all \(i,j\). Define \(f^-(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{f_i-Ld(x,x_i)\}\) and \(f^+(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}\{f_i+Ld(x,x_i)\}\). Both functions are \(L\)-Lipschitz and satisfy \(f^-(x_i)=f^+(x_i)=f_i\). Every \(L\)-Lipschitz extension \(g:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(g(x_i)=f_i\) obeys \(f^-(x)\le g(x)\le f^+(x)\) for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise Lipschitz-consistent sampled values generate lower and upper extremal Lipschitz extensions that interpolate the samples and bound every other Lipschitz extension pointwise.
assumptions_latex: \((D,d)\) is a metric space, \(L\ge0\), and \(S=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subset D\) is finite.
The data satisfy \(|f_i-f_j|\le Ld(x_i,x_j)\) for all \(i,j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functions \(f^-\) and \(f^+\) interpolate the samples, are \(L\)-Lipschitz, and satisfy \(f^-(x)\le g(x)\le f^+(x)\) for every admissible extension \(g\) and every \(x\in D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Interval-Arithmetic Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range enclosure by outward-rounded interval evaluation on a real box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n[\underline x_i,\overline x_i]\subset\mathbb R^n\), and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be represented by a finite expression using elementary operations and functions with available interval extensions. Replace each variable by its interval and evaluate every operation with outward rounding, requiring that every divisor interval exclude zero. The resulting interval \(F(X)=[\underline F(X),\overline F(X)]\) satisfies
\[
\{f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq F(X).
\]
Consequently, \(\underline F(X)\) is a valid lower bound and \(\overline F(X)\) is a valid upper bound for \(f\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outward-rounded interval evaluation encloses every objective value on a box, so its endpoints provide certified lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has an interval-evaluable expression on \(X\).
All interval operations are outward rounded.
No evaluated divisor interval contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\underline F(X)\le f(x)\le\overline F(X)\) for every \(x\in X\).

children.title: Centered-Form Bounds
children.top_down_role: Centered interval enclosures used within subdivision workflows.

knowledge_statements.title: Centered-Form Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order centered enclosure using an interval gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a box, choose \(c\in X\), and suppose \(f\) is continuously differentiable on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\). If \(G(X)\) is an interval vector satisfying \(\nabla f(x)\in G(X)\) for every \(x\in X\), then the centered form
\[
F_c(X)=f(c)+G(X)^{\mathsf T}(X-c)
\]
is an interval enclosure of the range of \(f\) on \(X\). Hence the endpoints of \(F_c(X)\) are certified objective bounds; repeated occurrences of variables in the original expression may be reduced because the expansion is anchored at the point \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding around a point and enclosing the gradient yields a certified first-order interval range bound with reduced dependency effects.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty box and \(c\in X\).
\(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(X\).
\(G(X)\) encloses every gradient on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq f(c)+G(X)^{\mathsf T}(X-c)\).

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of the gradient over X

children.title: Taylor-Form Bounds
children.top_down_role: Derivative-informed interval enclosures over search boxes.

knowledge_statements.title: Taylor-Form Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order interval Taylor enclosure on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a box, let \(c\in X\), and let \(f\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\). If \(H(X)\) is an interval matrix enclosing \(\nabla^2f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), then outward-rounded interval evaluation of
\[
T_2(X;c)=f(c)+\nabla f(c)^{\mathsf T}(X-c)+\tfrac12(X-c)^{\mathsf T}H(X)(X-c)
\]
encloses \(f(X)\). Its lower endpoint is therefore a certified lower bound for boxwise global optimization, and its upper endpoint is a certified upper range bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order expansion with an interval Hessian encloses the objective range and supplies certified boxwise bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty box and \(c\in X\).
\(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(X\).
\(H(X)\) encloses all Hessians on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq T_2(X;c)\).

children.title: Expansion-Point Selection
children.top_down_role: Centering choices that affect enclosure quality and computational cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Expansion-Point Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax choice of expansion point for box-centered remainder control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a box \(X=\prod_{i=1}^n[\underline x_i,\overline x_i]\), define its midpoint by \(m_i=(\underline x_i+\overline x_i)/2\). Among all expansion points \(c\in X\), the midpoint solves
\[
m\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in X}\max_{x\in X}\lVert x-c\rVert_\infty,
\qquad
\max_{x\in X}\lVert x-m\rVert_\infty=\max_i\frac{\overline x_i-\underline x_i}{2}.
\]
Thus, whenever a centered or Taylor remainder bound is nondecreasing in this maximum distance and no derivative information favors another point, choosing \(c=m\) minimizes the associated distance-based worst-case estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The box midpoint minimizes maximum infinity-norm distance to the box and therefore minimizes distance-based worst-case remainder estimates.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty bounded box.
The remainder estimate is nondecreasing in \(\max_{x\in X}\lVert x-c\rVert_\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The midpoint \(m\) minimizes the stated distance-based remainder estimate over \(c\in X\).

children.title: Remainder-Enclosure Quality
children.top_down_role: Dependency and overestimation effects limiting higher-order bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Remainder-Enclosure Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic control of second-order Taylor remainders by box radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be twice continuously differentiable on a convex neighborhood of a box \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\), choose \(c\in X\), and suppose \(\lVert\nabla^2 f(x)\rVert_2\le M\) throughout \(X\). For each \(x\in X\), the first-order Taylor remainder \(R(x;c)=f(x)-f(c)-\nabla f(c)^{\mathsf T}(x-c)\) satisfies
\[
|R(x;c)|\le\frac{M}{2}\lVert x-c\rVert_2^2.
\]
Therefore a sound remainder enclosure is \([ -Mr_c^2/2,Mr_c^2/2]\), where \(r_c=\max_{x\in X}\lVert x-c\rVert_2\); its width decreases quadratically as the box radius tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded Hessian gives a Taylor-remainder enclosure whose width is at most the Hessian bound times the squared box radius.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near the convex box \(X\).
\(\lVert\nabla^2 f(x)\rVert_2\le M\) for all \(x\in X\).
\(c\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(X;c)\subseteq[-Mr_c^2/2,Mr_c^2/2]\), whose width is \(Mr_c^2\).

notation.meaning: maximum Euclidean distance from c to X

children.title: Interval Newton Methods
children.top_down_role: Interval Newton contractors used for existence, uniqueness, or exclusion tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Box contraction and root testing through an interval linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a continuously differentiable map \(F:X\to\mathbb R^n\), a box \(X\), and a point \(c\in X\), compute an interval Jacobian \(J_F(X)\) enclosing every \(J_F(x)\). Obtain an interval vector \(D\) enclosing all solutions \(d\) of
\[
A d=F(c),\qquad A\in J_F(X),
\]
and define the interval Newton image \(N(X,c)=c-D\). Replace \(X\) by \(X^+=X\cap N(X,c)\). If \(X^+=\varnothing\), discard the box; if a prescribed width or residual tolerance is met, return \(X^+\); otherwise repeat or subdivide \(X^+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval Newton repeatedly intersects a box with a certified Newton image, excluding empty intersections and contracting boxes that may contain roots.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(X\).
\(J_F(X)\) encloses every Jacobian on \(X\).
The interval linear solver produces a sound enclosure \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every zero of \(F\) in \(X\) belongs to \(X^+=X\cap N(X,c)\).

children.title: Krawczyk Methods
children.top_down_role: Krawczyk-operator workflows for validated contraction and root assessment.

knowledge_statements.title: Krawczyk Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditioned interval fixed-point contraction for nonlinear systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a continuously differentiable map \(F:X\to\mathbb R^n\), choose \(c\in X\) and a nonsingular point matrix \(C\), typically approximating \(J_F(c)^{-1}\). With an interval Jacobian enclosure \(J_F(X)\), form
\[
K(X,c)=c-CF(c)+(I-CJ_F(X))(X-c)
\]
using outward-rounded interval arithmetic, and set \(X^+=X\cap K(X,c)\). Discard \(X\) when \(X^+=\varnothing\); return \(X^+\) when the required width or residual tolerance is achieved; otherwise repeat the Krawczyk contraction or subdivide the contracted box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Krawczyk method uses a point preconditioner and interval Jacobian to contract, exclude, or certify boxes containing nonlinear-system roots.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near \(X\).
\(J_F(X)\) encloses every Jacobian on \(X\).
\(C\) is a nonsingular real matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every zero of \(F\) in \(X\) remains in \(X^+=X\cap K(X,c)\).

children.title: Existence Certification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Validated uses that retain regions containing certified solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence Certification Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict self-inclusion tests certifying an isolated nonlinear-system root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable near a box \(X\), and let its interval Jacobian enclose all Jacobians on \(X\). For \(c\in X\), either of the strict inclusions
\[
N(X,c)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)
\quad\text{or}\quad
K(X,c)\subseteq\operatorname{int}(X)
\]
constitutes an existence certificate when the corresponding interval Newton or Krawczyk operator is sound. Under the standard nonsingularity conditions of the selected operator, the certificate establishes that \(F(x)=0\) has exactly one solution in \(X\). The inclusion can be checked entirely from outward-rounded interval endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict containment of a sound interval Newton or Krawczyk image inside the box certifies a unique root under the operator's nonsingularity conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near \(X\).
The chosen operator uses a sound interval Jacobian enclosure.
The chosen operator satisfies its standard nonsingularity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strict inclusion certifies existence and uniqueness of a zero of \(F\) in \(X\).

children.title: Exclusion Certification Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Exclusion Certification Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval tests proving that a box contains no system root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_n):X\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous, with interval component enclosures \(\mathcal F_i(X)\supseteq F_i(X)\). The box \(X\) contains no zero of \(F\) if at least one component satisfies \(0\notin\mathcal F_i(X)\). If a sound interval Newton or Krawczyk image is available, either condition
\[
X\cap N(X,c)=\varnothing
\quad\text{or}\quad
X\cap K(X,c)=\varnothing
\]
also certifies exclusion, because every zero in \(X\) must belong to the corresponding intersection. Each test is verifiable using outward-rounded interval endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box is root-free when a component range excludes zero or a sound Newton-type image has empty intersection with the box.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\mathcal F_i(X)\) soundly encloses the range of \(F_i\) on \(X\).
Any Newton or Krawczyk image used is sound for all zeros in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any displayed exclusion condition implies \(\{x\in X:F(x)=0\}=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: interval range enclosure for component i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One detailed interval Newton processing step that returns zero to four surviving boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a box $X$ and tolerance $\epsilon$, compute $\Phi(X)$. Terminate if $\|\Phi(X)\|<\epsilon$; if $0
otin\Phi(X)$, discard $X$. Otherwise compute $J(X)$, an approximate inverse $B$ of $\operatorname{mid}J(Y)$, and $M:=BJ(X)$. If $B$ is available, set $x:=\operatorname{mid}X$ and $b:=B\Phi(x)$, apply interval Gauss–Seidel to $M(x-Y)=b$, replace $X$ by the resulting $Y$, and record coordinate gaps. Repeat the simplified contraction while $X$ diminishes significantly, discarding it whenever $0
otin\Phi(X)$. When contraction stalls, split along one or two largest recorded coordinate gaps into two or four boxes and discard each $V_i$ satisfying $0
otin\Phi(V_i)$. If no usable gaps exist, or if $B$ cannot be computed, bisect $X$ normal to its longest edge (or by another criterion) and apply the same exclusion test. The iteration ends with zero to four boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the interval residual and discard the box if it cannot contain a zero. Otherwise form a preconditioned interval Newton system and repeatedly contract it by interval Gauss–Seidel while contraction remains significant. When contraction stalls, split along the largest recorded gaps; if gap splitting is unavailable or preconditioning fails, bisect the box. Residual tests discard child boxes that cannot contain a zero, leaving at most four boxes.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon>0
X\text{ is an interval box}
\Phi(X)\text{ and }J(X)\text{ are computable interval enclosures}
B\approx(\operatorname{mid}J(Y))^{-1}\text{ when this approximate inverse can be computed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration returns a collection }\{V_i\}_{i=1}^k\text{ with }0\le k\le4,\text{ after discarding every tested }V_i\text{ for which }0\notin\Phi(V_i).

children.title: Boxing Devices
children.top_down_role: Devices that contract or reshape interval search boxes.

knowledge_statements.title: Boxing Devices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound coordinatewise box reduction for constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible set \(S=\{x\in X:g_j(x)\in T_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), a boxing device is a map \(B\) from boxes to boxes that computes coordinatewise reduced intervals and satisfies
\[
B(X)\subseteq X,
\qquad
S\cap X\subseteq B(X).
\]
It may obtain each reduced coordinate by interval propagation, one-dimensional interval solves, or slicing tests, but it must use outward rounding. The output \(B(X)=\varnothing\) certifies infeasibility of \(X\); otherwise the reduced box retains every feasible point and can replace \(X\) before subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boxing device shrinks coordinate intervals without removing feasible points; an empty reduced box certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: All interval range and slicing tests used by \(B\) are sound.
The target sets \(T_j\) are represented exactly or by outward enclosures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(X)\subseteq X\) and \(S\cap X\subseteq B(X)\).

children.title: Subdivision Accelerators

knowledge_statements.title: Subdivision Accelerators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contract-before-branch workflow for interval subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a queue with the search box \(X_0\) and an incumbent upper bound \(U\). For each extracted box \(X\), apply sound contractors until a contraction stopping rule holds, obtaining \(C(X)\). Discard \(C(X)\) if it is empty or if its certified objective lower bound \(L(C(X))\) satisfies \(L(C(X))\ge U-\varepsilon\). Otherwise update \(U\) using feasible points; if the box width is at most the prescribed tolerance, return it as unresolved, and otherwise bisect a selected coordinate and enqueue both children. The accelerator is valid because contraction and pruning preserve every \(\varepsilon\)-competitive feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting and bounding boxes before bisection reduces the search tree while preserving every point that could improve the incumbent within tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Every contractor preserves feasible points.
\(L(X)\) is a certified lower bound on each box.
\(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pruned boxes contain no feasible point with objective value below \(U-\varepsilon\).

children.title: Contractor Composition
children.top_down_role: Coordination of multiple box-reduction devices.

knowledge_statements.title: Contractor Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of sound box contractors under sequential composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) be box contractors satisfying \(C_i(X)\subseteq X\) and \(S\cap X\subseteq C_i(X)\) for every box \(X\). Their sequential composition
\[
C=C_k\circ C_{k-1}\circ\cdots\circ C_1
\]
is also a sound contractor: \(C(X)\subseteq X\) and \(S\cap X\subseteq C(X)\). Repeated cyclic application therefore produces a nested sequence of boxes while retaining every point of \(S\) in the initial box. Iteration may stop at a common fixed point, an empty box, or a prescribed contraction tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential or cyclic composition of sound contractors remains sound, yields nested boxes, and preserves every feasible point.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) maps boxes to boxes.
Each \(C_i\) is contracting and preserves \(S\cap X\) for every box \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(X)\subseteq X\) and \(S\cap X\subseteq C(X)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(B=[0,1]\), \(f(x)=(x-1/2)^2\), and an incumbent \(U\in(0,1/4)\). Although the endpoint samples satisfy \(f(0)=f(1)=1/4>U\), the interior point \(x=1/2\) satisfies \(f(1/2)=0<U\). Hence a rule that rejects \(B\) solely because its sampled values exceed \(U\) can discard a box containing a better point. Safe acceleration therefore requires a certified lower bound, infeasibility proof, or exclusion contractor whose validity holds over all of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite samples cannot justify rejecting an entire box: poor endpoint values may coexist with a better interior point. Safe rejection requires a bound or contractor valid throughout the box.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic RLT relaxation of a polynomial program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers monomial lifting, omission of the nonlinear consistency identities, subbox lower bounds, and strengthening by valid product constraints. The source's stronger infeasibility assertion is not retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(f_i(x)=l_i(x)+\sum_{\alpha\in A}c_{i\alpha}x^\alpha\). Introducing \(y_\alpha=x^\alpha\) gives an equivalent lifted formulation with linear functions \(L_i(x,y)=l_i(x)+\sum_{\alpha\in A}c_{i\alpha}y_\alpha\) and nonlinear identities \(y_\alpha=x^\alpha\). Omitting these identities gives an LP relaxation \(LR(P_M)\) on each subbox \(M=[p,q]\subseteq[a,b]\), so \(\operatorname{val}(LR(P_M))\leq\operatorname{val}(P_M)\). If \(LR(P_M)\) is infeasible, then \(P_M\) is infeasible and, under the minimization convention, \(\operatorname{val}(LR(P_M))=+\infty\). Linearized products of factors known to be nonnegative on the feasible set yield valid strengthening inequalities, generally at increased formulation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing monomials by auxiliary variables gives an equivalent lifted problem when the monomial identities are retained. Dropping those identities gives an LP lower bound. Products of valid nonnegative constraint or bound factors can strengthen the relaxation. Infeasibility of the LP certifies infeasibility of the polynomial problem, but the converse need not hold.
assumptions_latex: f_i(x)=l_i(x)+\sum_{\alpha\in A}c_{i\alpha}x^\alpha,\quad i=0,\ldots,m
P:\ \min\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\geq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ a\leq x\leq b\}
M=[p,q]\subseteq[a,b]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(LR(P_M))\leq\operatorname{val}(P_M),\qquad LR(P_M)\text{ infeasible}\Rightarrow P_M\text{ infeasible}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A computational-graph representation of a factorable function \(f:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\). Its leaves are input coordinates or constants; every nonleaf node \(v\) is labeled by an admissible elementary operation \(\phi_v\) and satisfies \(z_v=\phi_v((z_u)_{u\in\operatorname{pred}(v)})\). A distinguished root \(r\) satisfies \(z_r=f(x)\) whenever all node operations are defined. Shared nodes may feed several successors, so the graph represents dependencies as well as an evaluation order.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a factorable model in \(x\), introduce one variable \(z_v\) for selected computational nodes and impose defining equations \(z_v=\phi_v((z_u)_{u\in\operatorname{pred}(v)})\). Replace every selected subexpression by its corresponding \(z_v\), including an objective root variable when desired. If \(L\) denotes the resulting lifted feasible set, then each original feasible \(x\) has a recursively determined lift \((x,z)\in L\), and every \((x,z)\in L\) projects to an original feasible point with the same objective value. Thus the reformulation is exact before any defining equality is relaxed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables replace selected subexpressions and are tied to them by defining equations. Before relaxation, projection recovers exactly the original feasible model and objective values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Expression disaggregation replaces a composite factorable relation by nodewise elementary relations. For each nonleaf computational node \(v\), introduce \(z_v\) and impose \(z_v=\phi_v((z_u)_{u\in\operatorname{pred}(v)})\); original variables supply leaf values, and the root variable replaces the composite expression in the model.
